case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a majority-group plaintiff bringing a Title VII discrimination claim must demonstrate 'background circumstances' suggesting the defendant is an unusual employer who discriminates against the majority, in addition to pleading all other standard elements of the claim.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, 42 U.S.C. 2000e et seq., which prohibits employment discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Marlean A. Ames, a majority-group plaintiff (white woman), argues that Title VII imposes a uniform evidentiary standard on all plaintiffs regardless of their majority or minority group status, and that requiring majority-group plaintiffs to satisfy an additional 'background circumstances' element creates an unequal, two-tiered system of pleading that is inconsistent with the statute's text, which protects all individuals equally from workplace discrimination.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The Ohio Department of Youth Services, supported by arguments raised in related briefing, contends that the Sixth Circuit's 'background circumstances' requirement is a legitimate and judicially manageable threshold showing that accounts for the statistical reality that majority-group members are less frequently subjected to discrimination, and further argues procedural vehicle flaws exist because Ames failed to challenge this element below and separately lost on the pretext prong of her demotion claim, making the question presented potentially non-dispositive.
key_precedents: McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green (establishing the burden-shifting framework for Title VII disparate treatment claims)
Texas Department of Community Affairs v. Burdine (clarifying the McDonnell Douglas framework and plaintiff's burden of establishing a prima facie case)
St. Mary's Honor Center v. Hicks (addressing pretext analysis under Title VII)
Reeves v. Sanderson Plumbing Products (addressing sufficiency of pretext evidence)
State v. Sum, 511 P.3d 92 (Wash. 2022) (cited by amicus regarding race-conscious legal standards in state courts)
Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard (implicitly relevant to equal protection principles cited by amici)

John Roberts.reasoning: The conference has reached a remarkable degree of consensus, and I find the core reasoning sound and consistent with my own minimalist approach. Justice Kagan's observation that the 'background circumstances' requirement introduces unpredictable, circuit-specific variations into what should be a uniform federal standard is particularly compelling from an institutional standpoint — the Court's legitimacy is best served by clear, administrable rules that apply equally to all litigants. Justice Kavanaugh correctly notes that allowing courts to calibrate pleading thresholds based on demographic group membership creates the appearance that Title VII protects some workers more than others, which undermines public confidence in the judiciary. As Chief Justice, I would assign the majority opinion with an eye toward the narrowest possible holding: that courts may not impose additional prima facie elements beyond those articulated in McDonnell Douglas based solely on a plaintiff's majority-group status, leaving for another day any broader questions about the precise contours of the prima facie case in reverse discrimination claims.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: I am in complete agreement with Justice Gorsuch and Justice Barrett that the text of 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1) admits of no ambiguity — 'any individual' means any individual, full stop, and no amount of sociological reasoning about which groups are statistically more likely to face discrimination can justify judicial addition of elements Congress never wrote into the statute. The strongest argument for the respondent would be that McDonnell Douglas itself was a judicial construction, so courts have inherent flexibility to calibrate its elements — but this argument fails because McDonnell Douglas was crafted to implement the statute's existing cause of action, not to create demographic tiers of protection that the statute affirmatively forecloses. As I noted in my own analysis, McDonald v. Santa Fe Trail Transportation Co. already resolved the core question: Title VII claims by majority-group members 'must be adjudicated upon the same standards,' and the Sixth Circuit's 'background circumstances' requirement is irreconcilable with that holding. Justice Sotomayor's practical concern about real plaintiffs being forced out of court before presenting evidence actually reinforces the textualist conclusion — the background circumstances test is itself the barrier that must be removed.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: I find myself in complete agreement with Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch that the statutory text of Title VII is dispositive here — 'any individual' means any individual, full stop, and courts have no license to add elements to a cause of action that Congress did not write. Justice Barrett correctly notes that McDonald v. Santa Fe Trail Transportation Co. already settled this question nearly fifty years ago, holding that Title VII's protections extend equally to majority-group members, which makes the Sixth Circuit's 'background circumstances' requirement not merely an unwarranted judicial invention but one that directly contradicts binding precedent. The strongest argument for the respondent would be that statistical realities justify calibrating pleading standards to the likelihood of actual discrimination, but as Justice Kagan rightly observes, this substitutes judicial speculation about group-level probabilities for the neutral statutory text — and Title VII's individual-focused framework, confirmed in O'Connor v. Consolidated Coin Caterers Corp., forecloses exactly that kind of demographic gatekeeping. A uniform McDonnell Douglas standard that applies equally regardless of the plaintiff's majority or minority status is not only textually compelled but practically superior, as it avoids the workability problems that have produced inconsistent circuit-specific variations in what should be a coherent federal framework.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I find myself in rare but genuine agreement with Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett on the textual foundation here: Title VII's protection of 'any individual' admits no demographic qualification, and the 'background circumstances' requirement is precisely the kind of judicially-invented gatekeeping that forces real workers — people with legitimate grievances — out of court before they can even present their evidence. Justice Jackson's point about Muldrow v. City of St. Louis (2024) is particularly apt and reinforces my view: this Court has consistently and recently corrected lower courts for adding non-textual requirements to Title VII claims, and the Sixth Circuit's additional threshold element is exactly that kind of unauthorized judicial amendment. The strongest argument for the respondent would be that statistical realities about discrimination patterns justify calibrating pleading thresholds — but as O'Connor v. Consolidated Coin Caterers Corp. makes clear, the prima facie case turns on individual circumstances, not demographic probabilities, and allowing courts to adjust evidentiary burdens based on group membership would normalize discrimination against certain groups by treating it as legally unremarkable. From my perspective as someone deeply concerned with access to justice for vulnerable populations, I recognize that today's majority-group plaintiff may be tomorrow's minority-group plaintiff in a different workplace context, and a uniform standard protects everyone.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: I find myself in complete agreement with the conference, and Justice Jackson's invocation of Muldrow v. City of St. Louis (2024) is particularly apt — that decision exemplifies this Court's consistent practice of correcting lower courts that add non-textual requirements to Title VII, and the 'background circumstances' test is precisely that kind of judicial accretion. Justice Thomas is correct that McDonald v. Santa Fe Trail Transportation Co. already resolved the core question: Title VII's protections apply to majority and minority group members on identical terms, and the Sixth Circuit's framework directly contradicts that holding. The strongest argument for respondent would be that some contextual showing is necessary to weed out frivolous claims and that statistical reality — that majority-group members face discrimination less frequently — justifies a calibrated threshold, but this argument fails on my pragmatic textualist methodology because McDonnell Douglas's existing framework already performs that filtering function through its requirement that the plaintiff show she was qualified and replaced by someone outside the protected class, making the 'background circumstances' element redundant at best and discriminatory in administration at worst. A uniform standard is both more faithful to the text and more workable across circuits.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: I find myself in complete agreement with Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett that the text of 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1) simply does not contain a 'background circumstances' requirement, and no amount of statistical reasoning or policy intuition can conjure one into existence — that is the legislature's job, not ours. Justice Kagan makes a point I find particularly worth emphasizing from a textualist standpoint: the 'background circumstances' test doesn't just lack textual support, it affirmatively introduces the kind of group-based differential treatment that Title VII was enacted to prohibit, creating a perverse irony where the anti-discrimination statute is administered in a discriminatory fashion. The strongest argument for the respondent would be that McDonnell Douglas was itself a judicial construction, so courts have some latitude to calibrate its elements — but that argument proves too much; McDonnell Douglas was a gap-filling exercise in the absence of direct evidence, not a license to add substantive threshold elements that vary by the plaintiff's demographic identity, and O'Connor v. Consolidated Coin Caterers Corp. confirms the framework turns on individual circumstances. With nine colleagues reaching the same textual conclusion through varying methodologies — from Justice Sotomayor's remedial purpose analysis to Justice Thomas's original public meaning — the convergence only reinforces that the Sixth Circuit's rule is indefensible under any serious interpretive approach.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: I find myself in complete agreement with Chief Justice Roberts that the cleanest, most institutionally defensible resolution is a narrow holding that courts may not graft additional pleading elements onto Title VII's uniform framework based on a plaintiff's majority or minority status. Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett's textualist analysis reinforces my own view — the word 'any individual' in Section 2000e-2(a)(1) admits of no qualification based on demographic group membership, and McDonald v. Santa Fe Trail Transportation Co. already settled that the same standards apply regardless of whether the plaintiff is a majority or minority group member. The strongest argument for the respondent would be a workability or institutional competence argument — that courts need some threshold mechanism to screen out implausible reverse discrimination claims — but as Justice Kagan correctly notes, the background circumstances test has itself proven unworkable, generating circuit-specific variations that undermine uniform federal administration of Title VII. From an institutionalist perspective, a rule that visibly treats some workers' discrimination claims as more legally credible than others based solely on their demographic identity would damage the Court's legitimacy by suggesting Title VII provides unequal protection, which is precisely the appearance we must avoid.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The conference has reached remarkable unanimity, and I find my colleagues' arguments reinforcing rather than challenging my own analysis. Justice Thomas correctly identifies that McDonald v. Santa Fe Trail Transportation Co. already resolved the core question — Title VII claims 'must be adjudicated upon the same standards' regardless of the plaintiff's majority or minority status, and the Sixth Circuit's 'background circumstances' requirement is simply irreconcilable with that holding. Justice Jackson's invocation of Muldrow v. City of St. Louis (2024) is particularly apt, as it demonstrates this Court's consistent pattern of correcting lower courts that add non-textual requirements to Title VII claims — the 'background circumstances' test is precisely the kind of judicial invention Muldrow condemned. As a textualist, I would emphasize that the strongest argument for respondent — that statistical realities justify differential pleading standards — is a policy argument that belongs to Congress, not to courts interpreting a statute whose text draws no such distinction; the word 'any' in Section 2000e-2(a)(1) admits of no majority/minority qualification, and judicial solicitude for one group's discrimination claims cannot be purchased at the cost of another group's equal access to the statutory framework.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I find myself in complete agreement with my colleagues across the ideological spectrum, which itself speaks to the strength of the textual foundation here. Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett, approaching this from a strict textualist methodology, reach the same destination I do through my pragmatic lens: Title VII's protection of 'any individual' admits no qualification based on majority or minority status, and McDonald v. Santa Fe Trail Transportation Co. already foreclosed the argument that white plaintiffs occupy a different legal footing. Justice Kagan's point about workability particularly resonates with me — the 'background circumstances' test has produced exactly the kind of unpredictable, circuit-specific chaos that undermines the uniform administration of federal civil rights law, which is a practical harm that falls hardest on ordinary workers who cannot predict whether their claims will survive threshold scrutiny. My background as a public defender reinforces what the text already commands: procedural fairness means equal access to the courts, and a rule that forces majority-group plaintiffs to prove their employer is 'unusual' before accessing the same framework available to minority plaintiffs is precisely the kind of judicially-erected barrier that Congress never authorized and that this Court should reject.

John Roberts.reasoning: The text of Title VII plainly protects 'any individual' from discrimination based on protected characteristics, and as McDonald v. Santa Fe Trail Transportation Co. established, the statute's protections apply equally to majority and minority group members alike. The Sixth Circuit's 'background circumstances' requirement creates precisely the kind of two-tiered, judicially-invented evidentiary standard that finds no support in the statutory text or in McDonnell Douglas itself, which was designed as a uniform burden-shifting framework. My preference for narrow rulings actually counsels strongly here — the cleanest, most institutionally defensible resolution is simply to hold that courts may not graft additional pleading elements onto Title VII's uniform framework based on a plaintiff's majority or minority status, as doing so substitutes judicial speculation about discrimination patterns for the neutral statutory text. While I am attentive to the respondent's procedural vehicle concerns, the question presented is sufficiently preserved and important enough to warrant resolution, and a narrow holding restoring evidentiary uniformity under McDonnell Douglas avoids broader constitutional questions that might otherwise arise.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of Title VII, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1), is unambiguous: it prohibits discrimination against 'any individual' because of race, color, religion, sex, or national origin, with no textual basis for distinguishing between majority and minority group plaintiffs. The Sixth Circuit's 'background circumstances' requirement is a judge-made addition to the statutory text that has no grounding in the original public meaning of the statute as enacted in 1964, and this Court has already held in McDonald v. Santa Fe Trail Transportation Co. that Title VII claims by white plaintiffs 'must be adjudicated upon the same standards as would be applicable' to minority plaintiffs. Bostock v. Clayton County further reaffirmed that Section 2000e-2(a)(1) 'works to protect individuals' and 'does so equally,' focusing on individual treatment rather than group membership. Creating a two-tiered pleading standard based on a plaintiff's majority or minority status is precisely the kind of judicial rewriting of statutory text that textualism forbids, and I would reject it categorically regardless of the statistical premises offered to justify it.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text of Title VII plainly prohibits discrimination 'because of' race, sex, or other protected characteristics without any qualification based on whether the plaintiff belongs to a majority or minority group. As the Court held in McDonald v. Santa Fe Trail Transportation Co., 'the same standards' apply to Title VII claims regardless of whether the plaintiff is a majority or minority group member, and McDonnell Douglas's prima facie framework applies equally to so-called 'reverse discrimination' claims. The Sixth Circuit's 'background circumstances' requirement imposes an additional, judicially-invented pleading burden on majority-group plaintiffs that finds no support in the statutory text, contradicts McDonald's explicit holding, and creates precisely the kind of unequal, two-tiered system that a textualist reading of Title VII forbids. Oncale v. Sundowner Offshore Services reinforces this conclusion by instructing that 'the text of the law controls' rather than judicial speculation about which groups Congress was most concerned about protecting.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Title VII's text protects 'any individual' from discrimination based on protected characteristics, and nothing in the statute's plain language permits courts to impose heightened pleading burdens on majority-group plaintiffs. The 'background circumstances' requirement creates precisely the kind of two-tiered justice system that undermines the statute's promise of equal protection for all workers — and from a practical standpoint, it erects an additional barrier that forces real people with legitimate claims out of court before they can even present their evidence. As McDonnell Douglas and Burdine make clear, the burden-shifting framework was designed as a procedural tool to help plaintiffs reach trial, not as a substantive gatekeeping mechanism calibrated to statistical assumptions about which groups are 'more likely' to face discrimination; O'Connor v. Consolidated Coin Caterers Corp. confirms that the prima facie case turns on individual circumstances, not demographic probabilities. Requiring majority-group plaintiffs to prove their employer is 'unusual' before they can even access the McDonnell Douglas framework imposes an extra-statutory burden that has no basis in the text, undermines the statute's remedial purpose, and most troublingly, normalizes discrimination against certain groups by treating it as legally unremarkable.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Title VII's text is unambiguous: it prohibits discrimination 'because of' race, sex, or other protected characteristics, and it protects 'any individual' without qualification as to majority or minority status. The 'background circumstances' requirement creates precisely the kind of two-tiered, judicially invented pleading standard that has no basis in the statute's text or in McDonnell Douglas itself, which established a burden-shifting framework designed to be a 'sensible, orderly way to evaluate the evidence' rather than a gatekeeping mechanism that varies by the plaintiff's demographic group. As a pragmatic textualist, I find it deeply problematic that courts have grafted an additional element onto the prima facie case for majority-group plaintiffs when Congress drew no such distinction—if anything, imposing a heightened threshold on white or heterosexual plaintiffs while exempting minority plaintiffs from the same showing is itself a form of the group-based differential treatment Title VII was designed to prohibit. The workability concerns cut against the background circumstances test as well, since it introduces unpredictable, circuit-specific variations into what should be a uniform federal standard, undermining the coherent administration of Title VII across the country.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The text of 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1) is unambiguous: it prohibits discrimination against 'any individual' 'because of such individual's race, color, religion, sex, or national origin.' The word 'any' is as broad and inclusive as language permits, and nowhere does the statute condition its protections on whether the plaintiff belongs to a majority or minority group. The Sixth Circuit's 'background circumstances' requirement is a judicial invention with no textual foundation — courts do not get to add elements to a statutory cause of action that Congress did not write, regardless of how statistically sensible such additions might seem as a policy matter. McDonnell Douglas itself established a burden-shifting framework designed to be a flexible, practical tool for ferreting out discriminatory intent, not a gatekeeping mechanism that varies based on the plaintiff's demographic identity; imposing a heightened threshold exclusively on majority-group plaintiffs contradicts both the statute's plain meaning and the equal-treatment principle that Title VII was enacted to vindicate.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Title VII's text protects 'any individual' from discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin, and neither the statute nor McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green contemplates a two-tiered evidentiary framework that imposes additional burdens on majority-group plaintiffs. The 'background circumstances' requirement created by the Sixth Circuit and other circuits is a judicially-invented gloss that has no basis in the statutory text and is inconsistent with the principle articulated in Texas Department of Community Affairs v. Burdine that the McDonnell Douglas framework is a procedural device to assist in the orderly evaluation of evidence, not a substantive amendment to Title VII's scope. As an institutionalist, I am concerned that allowing circuit courts to calibrate pleading thresholds based on a plaintiff's majority or minority group status would undermine the Court's legitimacy by creating the appearance that Title VII protects some workers more than others, contrary to Congress's clear intent of uniform individual protection. Practical workability also counsels against the background circumstances test, as courts have struggled to apply it consistently, and the simpler, uniform standard better serves judicial administration.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of Title VII, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1), is unambiguous: it prohibits discrimination against 'any individual' because of a protected characteristic, without qualification based on whether that individual belongs to a majority or minority group. As a textualist, I cannot countenance a judicially-grafted 'background circumstances' requirement that the statutory text simply does not contain and that creates a two-tiered pleading standard based solely on a plaintiff's demographic majority status. McDonald v. Santa Fe Trail Transportation Co., 427 U.S. 273 (1976), already settled that Title VII's protections extend equally to majority-group members, and McDonnell Douglas itself articulates a uniform burden-shifting framework that nowhere conditions a prima facie case on the plaintiff's group prevalence in the workforce. The Sixth Circuit's additional threshold element is a judicial invention untethered from statutory text, inconsistent with this Court's precedent, and impermissibly discriminates in the administration of a statute whose whole purpose is to prohibit discrimination based on protected characteristics.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Title VII's text, 42 U.S.C. 2000e-2(a)(1), prohibits discrimination 'because of' race without qualification or distinction based on the plaintiff's majority or minority status, and the Sixth Circuit's 'background circumstances' requirement imposes an additional, non-textual burden that Congress never authorized. The McDonnell Douglas framework, as this Court has repeatedly emphasized in Burdine and St. Mary's Honor Center, is merely a procedural device for structuring proof—it cannot be used to engraft substantive threshold requirements that effectively create a two-tiered system of justice based on the plaintiff's demographic identity. My background as a public defender reinforces my conviction that procedural fairness demands equal access to the courts for all claimants; a rule that requires white plaintiffs to clear a higher evidentiary hurdle before their discrimination claims can even be heard is precisely the kind of judicially-created barrier that this Court has consistently rejected, most recently in Muldrow v. City of St. Louis (2024), where the Court again corrected lower courts for adding non-textual requirements to Title VII claims. The practical consequence of affirming the Sixth Circuit would be to render Title VII's universal protection illusory for majority-group members, undermining both the statute's equal protection principles and Congress's clear intent to protect all individuals from workplace discrimination regardless of their group membership.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a majority-group plaintiff bringing a Title VII discrimination claim must demonstrate 'background circumstances' suggesting the employer is the unusual type that discriminates against majority-group members, in addition to pleading all other standard elements of the claim.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, 42 U.S.C. 2000e et seq., which prohibits employment discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Marlean A. Ames, a majority-group plaintiff (white woman), argues that Title VII imposes a uniform evidentiary standard on all plaintiffs regardless of their majority or minority group status, and that requiring majority-group plaintiffs to satisfy an additional 'background circumstances' element creates an unequal, two-tiered system of protection that is inconsistent with the statute's text, purpose, and the principle of equal protection under the law. She contends that Title VII's protections apply equally to all employees and that imposing a heightened pleading burden on majority-group plaintiffs effectively discriminates in the administration of anti-discrimination law itself.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The Ohio Department of Youth Services, as respondent, implicitly defends the Sixth Circuit's application of the 'background circumstances' test, arguing that the additional evidentiary requirement for majority-group plaintiffs is a judicially developed and contextually appropriate standard that reflects the statistical reality that majority-group members are less frequently targets of workplace discrimination, thereby serving as a reasonable threshold filter. The respondent also raises procedural vehicle concerns, noting that Ames failed to challenge the 'background circumstances' element in the lower courts and instead attempted to satisfy it, and further argues that the demotion claim was independently rejected on pretext grounds, making the Question Presented potentially moot or insufficiently dispositive of the case outcome.
key_precedents: McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green (1973) - established the burden-shifting framework for Title VII disparate treatment claims
Texas Department of Community Affairs v. Burdine (1981) - clarified the burden-shifting framework under Title VII
St. Mary's Honor Center v. Hicks (1993) - addressed the pretext stage of the McDonnell Douglas framework
Reeves v. Sanderson Plumbing Products, Inc. (2000) - addressed sufficiency of evidence at the pretext stage
State v. Sum, 511 P.3d 92 (Wash. 2022) - cited by amicus as an example of race-conscious legal standards being applied in state courts
Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard (2023) - implicitly referenced in the broader equal protection context raised by amici
Parker v. Baltimore & Ohio Railroad Co. (D.C. Cir. 1981) - origin of the 'background circumstances' test adopted by several circuits including the Sixth Circuit

John Roberts.reasoning: The unanimity of my colleagues across the ideological spectrum — from Justice Thomas's strict textualism to Justice Jackson's procedural fairness concerns — reinforces my view that the 'background circumstances' test is a judicially-created gloss with no grounding in Title VII's text or the McDonnell Douglas framework. Justice Kagan's observation that the uniform standard already accounts for evidentiary context at the inference-of-discrimination stage is particularly persuasive from a minimalist standpoint: it demonstrates that eliminating the Parker test does not leave employers without protection, because plaintiffs still must show circumstances giving rise to an inference of discrimination. My preference for narrow grounds counsels writing the majority opinion to hold simply that McDonnell Douglas applies uniformly to all Title VII plaintiffs without the additional 'background circumstances' element, grounded in the statute's text and Oncale, without reaching broader questions about restructuring the prima facie case framework altogether. As Chief Justice, I would assign this opinion to write narrowly on textual grounds, resisting any temptation to use this case as a vehicle for broader pronouncements about reverse discrimination doctrine or the continued vitality of McDonnell Douglas itself.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: My colleagues across the ideological spectrum have converged on the correct textual answer, and I find Justice Gorsuch's invocation of McDonald v. Santa Fe Trail Transportation Co. particularly apt — that precedent established over four decades ago that Title VII's protections apply with equal force to majority-group plaintiffs, making the Parker 'background circumstances' test not merely a judicial gloss but a direct contradiction of this Court's own holding. The strongest argument for Respondent would be that the McDonnell Douglas framework is itself a judicial construct, and courts therefore retain discretion to calibrate its elements to reflect real-world discrimination patterns — but this argument proves too much, because McDonnell Douglas was designed as a uniform evidentiary tool to serve the statute's text, not as a vehicle for courts to make sociological judgments about which groups deserve easier access to the courthouse. Justice Barrett correctly identifies that imposing differential burdens based on demographic group membership is precisely the kind of group-based differential treatment Title VII was enacted to prohibit, and no amount of empirical observation about historical discrimination patterns can authorize courts to rewrite a facially neutral statute. The text of § 2000e-2(a)(1) is unambiguous: it protects 'any individual' discriminated against 'because of' a protected characteristic, full stop.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: I find myself in complete agreement with Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch that the plain text of Title VII, as applied uniformly in McDonald v. Santa Fe Trail Transportation Co., simply does not permit courts to engraft additional threshold elements onto the McDonnell Douglas framework based on a plaintiff's majority-group status. Justice Barrett's point about the statute's reference to 'any individual' is particularly well-taken — Congress used universally inclusive language, and the Parker 'background circumstances' test is precisely the kind of judicial legislation that textualism forbids, regardless of whatever sociological assumptions motivated the D.C. Circuit's invention of that test. I note with some interest that even Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson, colleagues with whom I rarely agree on civil rights questions, have reached the same textual conclusion here, which reinforces that this is not a case where conservative and progressive methodologies diverge — the statute's text is simply unambiguous. The strongest argument for respondent would be that the McDonnell Douglas framework itself is a judicial construct and courts therefore have some latitude to calibrate its elements, but as Furnco Construction Corp. v. Waters made clear, that latitude cannot extend to substantive narrowing of Title VII's scope, and creating a two-tiered protection system based on demographic group membership is precisely such a narrowing.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I find myself in complete agreement with my colleagues across the ideological spectrum, which itself speaks to the strength of the textual and structural arguments here. Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett, approaching this from a textualist perspective, and Justice Jackson, approaching it from a concern for procedural fairness, all converge on the same conclusion: Title VII's text simply does not permit a two-tiered evidentiary system sorted by the plaintiff's demographic group membership. I want to emphasize what Justice Kagan correctly identifies — the McDonnell Douglas framework's 'inference of discrimination' standard is already flexible and context-sensitive enough to account for the evidentiary realities that the 'background circumstances' test was ostensibly designed to address, making that additional requirement both redundant and improperly exclusionary. From my perspective, the real-world harm is concrete: real workers with legitimate discrimination claims are being turned away at the courthouse door not because their evidence is insufficient, but because of which demographic group they belong to — and that is precisely the kind of unequal administration of justice that Title VII was enacted to prevent.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: I find myself in complete agreement with my colleagues across the ideological spectrum, which itself is telling — when Justice Thomas and Justice Sotomayor reach the same conclusion through their respective methodologies, the legal answer is likely correct. Justice Barrett's point about McDonald v. Santa Fe Trail Transportation Co. is particularly well-taken: this Court already held in 1976 that Title VII applies equally to majority and minority group members, making the 'background circumstances' test not merely a judicial invention but one that contradicts our own precedent. I would emphasize, as Justice Roberts suggests, that we should resolve this on the narrow textual ground that McDonnell Douglas's prima facie framework must be applied uniformly — the 'circumstances giving rise to an inference of discrimination' standard already does the contextual work that the 'background circumstances' test purports to do, making the latter both redundant and improperly exclusionary. The strongest argument for respondent would be that statistical reality justifies a threshold filter for majority-group plaintiffs, but this pragmatic concern is better addressed at the pretext stage and the ultimate merits, not by creating a gatekeeping element that Title VII's text simply does not authorize.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: I find myself in complete agreement with Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett that the plain text of Title VII, as confirmed by McDonald v. Santa Fe Trail Transportation Co., admits no distinction between majority and minority group plaintiffs — the statute says 'any individual' and courts have no license to add words Congress omitted. Justice Barrett's point about the 'background circumstances' test being a purely judicial invention from Parker v. Baltimore & Ohio Railroad is particularly well-taken; as a textualist, I cannot countenance lower courts effectively amending a federal statute by grafting on additional elements that neither Congress enacted nor this Court sanctioned. Justice Sotomayor's practical observation that this two-tiered system erects extra barriers for real people with legitimate claims reinforces the textual conclusion — the McDonnell Douglas framework was designed as a uniform evidentiary tool, and Furnco Construction Corp. v. Waters makes clear it was never meant to work a substantive narrowing of Title VII's scope. The strongest argument for respondent would be that the 'background circumstances' test merely reflects the practical reality that majority-group discrimination is statistically less common, but this is precisely the kind of sociological reasoning that courts must not use to override unambiguous statutory text — Congress wrote a facially neutral statute and it is not our role to rewrite it based on demographic assumptions.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: I find myself in complete agreement with Chief Justice Roberts's institutionalist framing: the cleanest path here is the straightforward textual ground that McDonnell Douglas must apply uniformly to all plaintiffs, without reaching broader questions about eliminating the prima facie case requirement altogether. Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch are correct that McDonald v. Santa Fe Trail Transportation Co. already confirmed Title VII's equal application regardless of majority or minority status, making the 'background circumstances' test not merely a judicial gloss but a direct contradiction of settled precedent. Justice Sotomayor's point about the practical unfairness of prejudging claims based on group membership reinforces my institutionalist concern: a patchwork of circuit-by-circuit differential standards corrodes the Court's legitimacy and the uniform administration of federal law. The respondent's strongest counterargument — that the background circumstances test merely reflects the practical reality that majority-group discrimination is statistically less common — fails because Title VII's text and our precedents do not permit courts to calibrate evidentiary burdens based on sociological assumptions about group-level discrimination rates, and the inference-of-discrimination element already does the necessary contextual work without imposing a categorical threshold.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: I find myself in complete agreement with the conference's unanimous assessment, and Justice Thomas's uncompromising textualist analysis most closely mirrors my own methodology: the plain text of 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1) prohibits discrimination against 'any individual' without qualification, and no canon of construction permits courts to engraft a demographic threshold element that Congress never enacted. Justice Kagan's pragmatic observation that the uniform 'inference of discrimination' standard already accounts for evidentiary context at the prima facie stage is particularly well-taken — it demonstrates that the 'background circumstances' test is not only textually indefensible but also functionally redundant where legitimate and improperly exclusionary where not. Justice Roberts's counsel toward a narrow ruling resonates with my own preference for deciding no more than necessary: we need not disturb the McDonnell Douglas framework broadly, but need only hold that its elements must be applied uniformly to all plaintiffs regardless of majority or minority status. The respondent's procedural vehicle concerns, while worth noting in the opinion, do not deprive the Court of a clean vehicle to resolve this entrenched circuit split on a question of significant importance to the uniform administration of federal anti-discrimination law.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I find myself in strong agreement with Justice Sotomayor's observation that the 'background circumstances' test 'effectively prejudges her claim based on group membership — the very evil Title VII was enacted to prevent,' which resonates deeply with my background as a public defender who has seen how procedural gatekeeping mechanisms can deny real people access to justice before their claims are ever heard on the merits. Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch's textualist arguments, while reaching the same destination through a different methodological route, reinforce my own textual analysis: the statute says 'any individual' and 'because of' without qualification, and Parker's judicial gloss has no statutory anchor. I would add that the practical consequences of the background circumstances test are particularly troubling — it requires courts to make threshold demographic judgments that are both administratively unworkable and substantively corrosive to the uniform administration of anti-discrimination law, creating a system where the anti-discrimination statute itself discriminates in its application. The strongest argument for respondent — that procedural vehicle concerns about waiver and the independent pretext ruling on the demotion claim counsel against reaching the question — does not overcome the fact that the circuit split on this fundamental statutory question is genuine, entrenched, and demands resolution.

John Roberts.reasoning: Title VII's text prohibits discrimination 'because of' race, sex, and other protected characteristics without any textual basis for distinguishing between majority and minority group plaintiffs, and as the Court recognized in Oncale v. Sundowner Offshore Services, the statute's protections extend to all covered individuals regardless of whether they belong to a historically disfavored group. The 'background circumstances' test, originating in Parker v. Baltimore & Ohio Railroad, was a judicially-created gloss that effectively imposes a heightened pleading burden on majority-group plaintiffs with no grounding in the McDonnell Douglas framework itself — which, as Furnco Construction Corp. v. Waters clarified, was never intended to work a substantive narrowing of Title VII's scope. My preference for narrow rulings counsels resolving this case on the straightforward textual ground that McDonnell Douglas's prima facie framework must be applied uniformly across all plaintiffs, without endorsing broader arguments about eliminating the prima facie case requirement altogether, thereby preserving institutional legitimacy while correcting a clear circuit-created inequality. The respondent's procedural vehicle concerns, while not frivolous, do not deprive this Court of a clean vehicle to resolve a genuine and entrenched circuit split on an important question of federal statutory law.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The plain text of 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1) prohibits discrimination 'because of' race, color, religion, sex, or national origin without any qualification distinguishing majority-group from minority-group plaintiffs — the statute is facially neutral and applies with equal force to all employees regardless of their demographic status. The judicially invented 'background circumstances' requirement, originating in Parker v. Baltimore & Ohio Railroad Co. (D.C. Cir. 1981), has no grounding in the statutory text and represents precisely the kind of judicial legislation that textualism forbids; courts are not empowered to engraft additional elements onto a statute's plain meaning based on sociological assumptions about which groups are more likely to face discrimination. McDonnell Douglas itself established a burden-shifting framework as a practical evidentiary tool, not as a vehicle for creating a two-tiered system of statutory protection, and nothing in that precedent or its progeny — Burdine, Hicks, or Reeves — authorizes differential pleading burdens based on the plaintiff's majority or minority status. As this Court recognized in Adarand and as reinforced by Students for Fair Admissions, the principle of equal treatment under anti-discrimination law does not permit courts to impose heightened burdens on plaintiffs solely because of their racial or demographic group membership.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text of Title VII, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a), prohibits discrimination 'because of' race, sex, or other protected characteristics without any textual distinction between majority and minority group plaintiffs — the statute is facially neutral and applies equally to all individuals. The judicially-created 'background circumstances' test from Parker v. Baltimore & Ohio Railroad represents precisely the kind of judicial amendment to statutory text that textualism forbids; McDonnell Douglas itself, as clarified in Furnco Construction Corp. v. Waters, was never intended to impose substantive limitations on Title VII's scope but merely to provide an evidentiary framework for inferring discriminatory intent. Requiring a white plaintiff like Ames to satisfy an additional threshold element that a minority plaintiff need not satisfy creates a two-tiered system of statutory protection that has no basis in the statute's text and effectively discriminates in the administration of an anti-discrimination law — a result that is both textually indefensible and practically corrosive to the rule of law. While I am generally skeptical of expansive readings of civil rights statutes, here the correct textualist result actually narrows judicial overreach by eliminating a judge-made element that has no statutory foundation.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Title VII's text prohibits discrimination 'because of' race, sex, and other protected characteristics without any qualification based on the plaintiff's majority or minority group status, and McDonnell Douglas itself emphasized that the prima facie case requirements are 'not onerous' and 'minimal,' as reaffirmed in Burdine. Imposing an additional 'background circumstances' burden exclusively on majority-group plaintiffs creates precisely the kind of two-tiered, unequal system of justice that undermines the statute's core promise of equal protection in the workplace — and from a practical standpoint, it erects an extra barrier for real people with legitimate discrimination claims before they can even reach the merits of their case. The 'background circumstances' test, originating in Parker v. Baltimore & Ohio Railroad, was a judicial invention untethered to Title VII's text and inconsistent with this Court's repeated instruction that the McDonnell Douglas framework is flexible and context-sensitive, not a rigid gatekeeping mechanism that sorts plaintiffs by demographic category. Requiring Ames to demonstrate that her employer is an 'unusual' discriminator before she can even establish a prima facie case effectively prejudges her claim based on group membership — the very evil Title VII was enacted to prevent — and I would hold that all Title VII plaintiffs must satisfy the same uniform standard of showing adverse action under circumstances giving rise to an inference of discrimination.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Title VII's text prohibits discrimination 'because of' race, sex, and other protected characteristics without any qualification based on whether the plaintiff belongs to a majority or minority group, and the statute's plain language simply does not support a two-tiered evidentiary framework. The McDonnell Douglas prima facie case, as clarified in Burdine, requires only that a plaintiff demonstrate adverse action 'under circumstances which give rise to an inference of unlawful discrimination' — a flexible, context-sensitive standard that this Court has repeatedly emphasized should be 'minimal' and 'not onerous,' never a rigid checklist supplemented with additional elements for particular plaintiff classes. The 'background circumstances' test invented in Parker v. Baltimore & Ohio Railroad imposes a threshold burden that has no textual anchor in Title VII and effectively creates a discriminatory administration of anti-discrimination law itself — a result that is both textually indefensible and practically unworkable, as it requires courts to make threshold demographic judgments before even reaching the merits. As a pragmatic matter, the uniform standard already accounts for evidentiary context at the inference-of-discrimination stage, making the 'background circumstances' element redundant where it is satisfied and improperly exclusionary where it is not.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The plain text of Title VII, 42 U.S.C. 2000e-2(a)(1), prohibits discrimination against 'any individual' because of race, color, religion, sex, or national origin — Congress drew no distinction between majority and minority group members, and courts have no license to engraft additional elements onto a statute that the legislature did not authorize. As this Court confirmed in McDonald v. Santa Fe Trail Transportation Co., 427 U.S. 273 (1976), Title VII's protections apply equally regardless of whether the plaintiff belongs to a majority or minority group, making the 'background circumstances' test a judicially invented, two-tiered regime that directly contradicts the statute's uniform text. The McDonnell Douglas framework, while itself a judicial construct, was designed as a uniform evidentiary tool to assist all plaintiffs in proving the ultimate statutory question — whether an adverse action occurred 'because of' a protected characteristic — and nothing in that framework or its animating precedents authorizes courts to impose a heightened threshold burden on plaintiffs solely because of their demographic group membership. Applying the rule of lenity and my commitment to separation of powers, I would not permit lower courts to effectively amend Title VII by creating differential pleading standards that Congress never enacted and that this Court has never sanctioned.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Title VII's text prohibits discrimination 'because of' race, sex, or national origin without any qualification based on whether the plaintiff belongs to a majority or minority group, and McDonnell Douglas established a burden-shifting framework intended as a uniform evidentiary tool, not a substantive amendment creating tiered protection. The 'background circumstances' test, originating in Parker v. Baltimore & Ohio Railroad (D.C. Cir. 1981), is a judicially invented addition that has no grounding in the statute's text or this Court's precedents, and as Furnco Construction Corp. v. Waters (1978) clarified, the McDonnell Douglas method was never meant to work a substantive narrowing of Title VII's protections. From an institutionalist standpoint, permitting circuits to impose differential pleading burdens based on a plaintiff's majority-group status creates an unworkable, unprincipled patchwork that undermines the Court's legitimacy and the uniform administration of federal anti-discrimination law. Practical workability and fidelity to statutory text both counsel in favor of a single, uniform standard under which all Title VII plaintiffs must demonstrate circumstances giving rise to an inference of discrimination, without the additional 'background circumstances' hurdle imposed only on majority-group members.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of Title VII, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1), prohibits discrimination against 'any individual' based on protected characteristics, with no textual basis for imposing differential evidentiary burdens depending on whether the plaintiff belongs to a majority or minority group. As a textualist and originalist, I must follow the statute's plain meaning, which the Court confirmed in McDonald v. Santa Fe Trail Transportation Co. (1976) when it held that Title VII's protections apply equally to majority and minority group members and that the McDonnell Douglas framework applies uniformly to all plaintiffs. The judicially invented 'background circumstances' test, originating in Parker v. Baltimore & Ohio Railroad Co. (D.C. Cir. 1981), has no grounding in the statutory text or in McDonnell Douglas itself, and creating a two-tiered evidentiary system based on a plaintiff's demographic group membership is precisely the kind of group-based differential treatment that Title VII was enacted to prohibit. The respondent's procedural vehicle concerns, while not frivolous, do not overcome the fundamental legal error embedded in the Sixth Circuit's framework, particularly given that the question presented is squarely implicated by the record.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Title VII's text prohibits discrimination 'because of' race, sex, and other protected characteristics without any qualification based on the plaintiff's majority or minority group status, and as the Court recognized in Oncale v. Sundowner Offshore Services, the statute's plain text controls over judicial speculation about legislative intent. The 'background circumstances' test originating in Parker v. Baltimore & Ohio Railroad creates precisely the kind of two-tiered, unequal procedural burden that undermines Title VII's uniform protective framework established in McDonnell Douglas and clarified in Burdine — requiring majority-group plaintiffs to clear an additional threshold that minority-group plaintiffs need not satisfy is inconsistent with the statute's equal application to all employees. From my perspective as someone deeply attentive to procedural fairness and equal protection in the administration of law, it is particularly troubling that the mechanism designed to combat discrimination itself operates discriminatorily by imposing differential burdens based on group membership. The respondent's procedural vehicle concerns about waiver and the independent pretext ruling on the demotion claim do not overcome the fundamental statutory question, which the Court should resolve cleanly in favor of a uniform pleading standard for all Title VII plaintiffs regardless of majority or minority status.
